The approach to EVSE characterization is like that used in the NextGen Profiles project to test 350-kW DC fast chargers so that results produced by both projects are comparable [11]. This work focused on comparatively low-power DC fast chargers in the 20- to 30-kW range. The tests performed fall into one of two categories: EVSE characterization or vehicle characterization. 3.1.1 EVSE Characterization EVSE characterization tests are explained in detail in Appendix A and include EVSE Nominal Power Transfer, EVSE High-Utilization Characterization, and Off-Nominal Grid Input. These tests utilize NLR’s charge control box hardware to emulate the vehicle interface and allow for more custom charge sessions to be requested of the EVSE than would be possible with an EV. These results inform the development of CHIL physics models to ensure each CHIL device can individually emulate a charge session as influenced by the conditions addressed in these characterization tests. 3.1.2 Vehicle Characterization The vehicle characterization tests are meant to collect transfer functions that include specific EVSE hardware and EVs for use in the CHIL test environment in addition to vehicle response to Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) power curtailment requests. Appendix A.6 lists all the data required for vehicle and EVSE tests in detail. 3.2 Test Bed Setup The test bed, as outlined in Figure 5, incorporated several key components, including an EV, EVSE, and measurement tools such as the DL950, WT1806 power analyzer, CCS listener, and CANalzyer. Our measurements included monitoring the input power of the EVSE to assess AC power quality. Additionally, some EVSE enabled us to measure their output signals, such as DC voltage and current.
